title: Organizing Capitalism’s Discarded People: The Young Patriot Organization
author: Ron Jacobs
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-12-at-4.25.05-PM-680x483.png)

Cover art for the book It Is Not Enough to Survive: The Young Patriots Story
by Jesse Montgomery

If I were to guess, I would say that the first time I heard about the leftist
group called the Young Patriot Organization was in the winter of 1970-1971. It
was via an article in an underground newspaper lent to me by a friend who
subscribed to two or three of these papers and shared them with like-minded
folks in our high school. I recall seeing a picture of some white guys hanging
out with a couple Black Panthers in Chicago. The accompanying article talked
about an attempt by various leftist groups in Chicago working together as
community organizers with a revolutionary intent. I was intrigued but the fact
that I was living on a military base in Germany meant that I didn’t pay much
attention to the project or the Young Patriot Organization beyond the
occasional mention in a newspaper. By the time I got back to the United
States, the group no longer existed and, as I would soon discover—there were
other organizations whose members were beginning to get jobs in factories,
warehouses and the like with the intention of organizing young working-class
people. Those groups included the Revolutionary Union and several other
Marxist-Leninist organizations that would eventually be lumped into one
amalgam called the New Community Movement.

Recently, author and historian Jesse Montgomery’s history of the Young Patriot
Organization, titled [_It Is Not Enough to Survive: The Young Patriots
Story_](https://uncpress.org/9781469693965/it-is-not-enough-to-survive/), was
published by University of North Carolina Press. The text is well-researched,
tightly composed and a deep look into the organization, the times and place it
originated and evolved in, and a discussion of the meaning of culture, class,
identity politics and community. Straightforward in its telling, I _t is Not
Enough to Survive_ explores a time and consciousness when the political
leanings of white-skinned refugees from the Appalachian region in the US
South—hillbillies, if you will—were straying from their historically assumed
place on the right side of the US political spectrum. Of course, this
assumption of their conservatism did have its exceptions—the histories of the
coal miners and their struggles to unionize and fight the coal barons being
the most well-known, but not the only such history of defiance. Still, it was
the migration from the southern US to the wartime factories of the urban north
that provoked, in a manner similar to, but different, the more documented
northern migration of African-Americans during the same period. Both groups
were leaving sharecropping and an essentially feudal economic existence behind
while hoping to find a decent paying job in the rapidly expanding industrial
shops of wartime and then postwar capitalism. Unsurprisingly, many migrants
didn’t find a pot of gold. Instead, they found themselves in urban ghettoes
working day labor and thinking about the life they had left behind; a life
that like the country songs that romanticized it seemed better than it did
when they were actually living it.

Then came the 1960s. Anti-racist protests and civil rights legislation, anti-
poverty programs and urban renewal, a counterculture that rejected mainstream
values and the US war in Vietnam. It was probably the war that turned more
youth against the designs of the US government and the war machine it served
than anything else. More specifically, it was military conscription that was
the catalyst. As the war escalated and the draft took more and more young men
from their lives and dreamed-of futures, opposition to both also grew. Still,
most working- class men went when the letter from the draft board came; many
students, meanwhile, figured out a way to postpone or avoid the draft
completely. This was the scenario from which the Young Patriot organization
was birthed.

Montgomery relates this history in vivid detail. He begins by discussing the
decision by elements in the Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) to
organize in urban working- class neighborhoods under a project with the
acronym ERAP (Economic Research and Action Project). From this beginning, a
group calling itself Jobs or Income Now (JOIN) set up shop in Chicago’s Uptown
neighborhood. At first, it was only the outsiders doing the organizing; they
focused on tenants’ rights, unsafe housing, feeding people and assisting in
fighting for welfare rights. Intent on getting locals to join them, the JOIN
organizers held meetings, block parties and other protests against police
brutality. Slowly, but surely local youth and adults joined the organization.
Eventually, however, class differences and issues related to those differences
caused a split. The middle-class organizers left and soon the Young Patriots
Organization was formed. It was a heady time for leftist politics in the late
1960s and early 1970s. It was also a time when the growing power of the
left—especially groups like the SDS, Black Panthers, Young Patriots, Young
Lords and others—was freaking out the authorities across the board from the
Chicago police to the FBI and even into the CIA and White House. _It Is Not
Enough to Survive_ relates these phenomena with detailed and animated
descriptions. Likewise, the text describes interpersonal relations between the
group’s leaders, the group and the community, the group and other leftist
organization like the Black Panthers, and the repercussions of the conflicts
that arose. In his telling, Montgomery discusses the theory that accompanied
the Young Patriots’ praxis and reflects on potential meanings and lessons.
Important in these discussions is the formation and growth of the first
Rainbow Coalition; a coalition whose potential was almost certainly one reason
for the government’s assassination of its originator, Fred Hampton. (The
Coalition faltered in the wake of such grotesque state repression.) Speaking
of lessons, let me interject that not only is this a history and a case study,
this book is also an organizing manual with applications and implications for
today.

Montgomery doesn’t just tell a history in his text. Indeed, two of his
chapters discuss something not found in enough left-leaning texts of today.
That something is culture and its role in organizing for social justice and
ultimately revolutionary change. The Young Patriot Organization, like many
other youth groups of the period and leftist groups in history, considered
(knew?) the importance of culture in their organizing. Understanding culture
as contested territory, many new left organizations accepted and encouraged
the growth of the 1960s counterculture. From the Yippies and their vision of a
Woodstock Nation to Weatherman/Weather Underground’s somewhat clumsy (at least
in the beginning) adaptation of the counterculture to the Panthers’ conscious
rejection of what they called porkchop nationalism in favor of the Panthers’
revolutionary nationalism, the understanding of the importance of culture was
obvious. For the Young Patriot Organization, the question was how to take the
hillbilly culture already so important to the people they were organizing and
make it part of the revolutionary culture they hoped to inspire. Montgomery’s
discussion includes a consideration of why the group used and then rejected
the so-called Confederate flag—a discussion that reflects the confusion around
the flag’s meaning in the time period. In a chapter titled “Sing Me Back
Home,” after the Merle Haggard song about a prisoner on death row and his last
request, Montgomery provides one of the most comprehensive and perceptive
discussions of US country music and its meaning I’ve read in a long time.

Jesse Montgomery has done us a big favor in writing this book. In a historical
moment when the far right seems insurmountable and the US public has forgotten
how to put up the kind of fight required to put the far right back in the
darkened cave it wants us all to exist in, this history of the Young Patriots
and the circumstances of their all-too-brief existence provides hope and
instruction. Fascism may be rearing its ugly head today in a manner even
uglier than that which existed in the repression of the late 1960s and early
1970s, but that doesn’t mean it can’t be defeated. After all, it must be.
